### 1.  What an operation can do  

Write a binary word \(x=x_{1}x_{2}\dots x_{n}\) as  

\[
\bigl(x_{1},\;d_{1},d_{2},\dots ,d_{n-1}\bigr),\qquad 
d_{i}= \begin{cases}
0 & (x_{i}=x_{i+1})\\[2pt]
1 & (x_{i}\neq x_{i+1})
\end{cases}
\]

The first coordinate tells the first digit, the sequence
\((d_{1},\dots ,d_{n-1})\) tells where a *run* (a maximal block of equal
digits) begins.  
For a word of length \(n\) there are at most \(n-1\) such “boundary’’
entries.

A **deletion** of a contiguous block of equal digits removes that block
and joins the two neighbours.  Only the two boundaries that touched the
deleted block can change (they may turn from 1 to 0 or from 0 to 1), and
the first digit may change only if the deletion starts at the left end.
Thus a single deletion can modify **at most two** of the coordinates of the
pair \((x_{1},d_{1},\dots ,d_{n-1})\).

An **insertion** of a block of equal digits has exactly the same effect:
it creates at most two new boundaries (or removes two if the block is
inserted between equal digits) and may change the first digit when the
block is inserted at the front.  Hence one insertion also changes at most
two coordinates.

Consequently, each allowed operation can correct at most two mismatches
between two words when they are compared in this representation.
